limit.title: Limit
limit.definition: The limit of $f$ at $a$ is $L$ if $f(x)$ can be made arbitrarily close to $L$ by taking all $x$ sufficiently close to $a$, with $x\ne a$.
limit.idea: Trace the graph toward the same input from the left and the right. Even if there is a hole, the two branches can point to the same height. That height is what the limit records.

parts.title: Defined near a point
parts.definition: A function is defined near $a$ if its domain contains every point of some open interval about $a$, except possibly $a$ itself.
parts.idea: The expression $(x^2-1)/(x-1)$ has a hole at $1$. You can still approach it through inputs on both sides.
parts.aliases: defined near a point domain open interval

parts.title: Limits and function values
parts.definition: Changing only the value at the point leaves the limit unchanged.
parts.idea: Imagine moving the filled point at $x=2$ straight up. Which part of the graph would a traveler approaching from either side see change?

figure.alt: A rising line has an open circle at (2, 4) and a separate filled point at (2, 7).
figure.prompt: What happens to $\lim_{x\to2}g(x)$ if the filled point moves higher? What happens to $g(2)$?
figure.reasoning: The nearby line stays fixed, so the limit remains $4$. The filled point currently gives $g(2)=7$, and moving it changes that value.

parts.reasoning: The nearby graph follows $y=x+2$, so its limit at $2$ is $4$. The filled point gives $g(2)=7$.

parts.title: Graph method
parts.definition: Trace the graph toward the input from each side. Read the function value from the filled point.
parts.idea: Start on a branch away from the marked input and trace toward it. Repeat from the other side before reading the filled dot.

figure.alt: At input −1, a descending line has an open circle at height 1 and a filled point above it at height 3.
figure.prompt: Use the graph to find $f(-1)$ and the two one-sided limits at $-1$. Is $f$ continuous there?
figure.reasoning: The filled point gives $f(-1)=3$. The two branches both approach $1$, so the limit is $1$ and $f$ is discontinuous at $-1$.

parts.title: Table method
parts.definition: Choose inputs approaching $a$ from both sides and compare the corresponding outputs.
parts.idea: Use inputs on both sides. In the hole example, the table suggests a height, and factoring explains why every sufficiently close input gives an output near that height.

parts.title: Oscillation
parts.definition: The values of $\sin(1/x)$ keep returning to both $1$ and $-1$ arbitrarily close to zero.
parts.idea: Even very close to zero, the graph keeps reaching a peak and then a trough. Compare those heights before trusting a short table.
parts.reasoning: Arbitrarily close to $0$, some inputs give $\sin(1/x)=1$ and others give $\sin(1/x)=-1$. There is no single limiting height.

figure.alt: The graph of sine of one over x makes increasingly frequent oscillations between −1 and 1 on approach to zero.
figure.prompt: Does $\sin(1/x)$ approach a single value as $x\to0$? Use what happens near its peaks and troughs.
figure.reasoning: Arbitrarily close to $0$ there are inputs with output $1$ and others with output $-1$. The finite limit does not exist.

limit.example: For $f(x)=\frac{x^2-4}{x-2}$, the graph follows $y=x+2$ up to the hole at $(2,4)$. Thus $\lim_{x\to2}f(x)=4$.

figure.alt: The line through the horizontal axis at −2 has an open circle at (2, 4).
figure.prompt: Read the graph. What is $\lim_{x\to2}f(x)$? Is $f(2)$ defined?
figure.reasoning: Both sides approach $4$. The open circle leaves $f(2)$ undefined.

sides.title: One-sided limits
sides.definition: A left-hand limit uses inputs below $a$. A right-hand limit uses inputs above $a$.
sides.idea: A piecewise formula can draw two branches that meet at different heights. Approaching along each branch tells you whether there is a single height to report.

parts.title: Left- and right-hand limits
parts.definition: The superscript on $a$ gives the side from which the input approaches.
parts.idea: In a piecewise rule, $x\to0^-$ tells you which formula to read before you substitute. The rule assigned to $x=0$ may be a third formula.

figure.alt: At input zero, a line approaches an open point at height 2 from the left. A curved branch starts at a filled point at height −3 on the right.
figure.prompt: Approach $0$ from each side of the graph. Do the two branches lead you to the same height?
figure.reasoning: The left-hand limit is $2$ and the right-hand limit is $-3$. The two-sided limit does not exist.

parts.title: Two-sided limit criterion
parts.definition: The two-sided limit is $L$ exactly when both one-sided limits equal $L$.
parts.idea: Cover the filled point and follow the two branches. If they head to the same height, moving the filled point cannot change the two-sided limit.

figure.alt: Two branches approach an open circle at the origin. A filled point lies above them at (0, 2).
figure.prompt: Does $\lim_{x\to0}g(x)$ exist here? How does it compare with $g(0)$?
figure.reasoning: Both branches approach zero, so $\lim_{x\to0}g(x)=0$. The separate filled point gives $g(0)=2$.

parts.title: The case method
parts.definition: Use a separate formula on each side of the input.
parts.idea: In $\frac{x^2-4}{\lvert x-2\rvert}$, write the absolute value separately on each side of $2$. Keep the minus sign from the left branch when canceling.

sides.example: For $h(x)=\frac{x^2-4}{\lvert x-2\rvert}$, the left-hand limit at $2$ is $-4$ and the right-hand limit is $4$.

laws.title: Limit laws
laws.definition: Suppose $f(x)\to L$ and $g(x)\to M$ as $x\to a$, with $L$ and $M$ finite. Apply the limit law for each operation in the formula.
laws.idea: Once the limits of $f$ and $g$ are known, use the operations in the formula to assemble the answer. A quotient or an even root calls for one extra check.

parts.title: Constants, sums, and differences
parts.definition: The limits of a constant and the identity are $c$ and $a$. Add or subtract finite limits and carry constant factors through.
parts.idea: Read $3x^2-2x+1$ term by term. The coefficient stays with its term, and the final constant contributes its own value.

parts.title: Products and quotients
parts.definition: Multiply the limits of the factors. For a quotient, the denominator limit must be nonzero.
parts.idea: Write down the limit of the denominator before dividing. If it is zero, the quotient law cannot tell you the height.

parts.title: Powers and roots
parts.definition: Positive integer powers and roots preserve finite limits wherever the roots are defined.
parts.idea: In $\frac{\sqrt{f(x)-1}}{(g(x))^2}$, work from the inside out. Check the quantity under the root and the limiting denominator before combining the pieces.

laws.example: The sum, scalar multiple, and power laws give $\lim_{x\to2}(3x^2-2x+1)=9$.

squeeze.title: Squeeze theorem
squeeze.definition: If a function lies between a lower and an upper bound near $a$, and both bounds tend to $L$, then the function tends to $L$.
squeeze.idea: Even when the middle formula is unknown, its graph must fit between the two bounds. If both approach the same height, the middle graph has nowhere else to go.

parts.title: Squeezing an oscillating function
parts.definition: Multiply the bounds $-1\le\sin(1/x)\le1$ by $x^2\ge0$.
parts.idea: Draw the two parabolas $y=-x^2$ and $y=x^2$. How much room remains for the oscillations between them as $x$ approaches zero?

figure.alt: The curve oscillates between the parabolas y = −x squared and y = x squared, which meet at the origin.
figure.prompt: Which two functions bound $x^2\sin(1/x)$? Use them to find its limit as $x\to0$.
figure.reasoning: Since $-1\le\sin(1/x)\le1$ and $x^2\ge0$, the graph stays between $-x^2$ and $x^2$. Both bounds tend to zero.

parts.reasoning: For $x\ne0$, $-x^2\le x^2\sin(1/x)\le x^2$. Both bounds tend to $0$, so the middle function tends to $0$.

parts.title: The fundamental trigonometric limit
parts.definition: For an angle measured in radians, sine divided by its argument tends to one as the angle tends to zero.
parts.idea: Compare the triangle inside the unit-circle sector with the larger triangle outside. Measuring the angle in radians lets those area bounds control $\frac{\sin\theta}{\theta}$.

figure.alt: A radius at angle θ meets the unit circle at P and the vertical tangent at T. The sector lies between an inscribed triangle and the larger triangle reaching T.
figure.prompt: For $0<\theta<\pi/2$, compare the areas of the smaller triangle, the unit-circle sector, and the larger triangle. What inequality follows?
figure.reasoning: The areas give $\frac12\sin\theta\le\frac12\theta\le\frac12\tan\theta$. Rearranging gives $\cos\theta\le\frac{\sin\theta}{\theta}\le1$.

parts.title: Match the argument
parts.definition: Rewrite the denominator so it matches the angle inside sine.
parts.idea: In $\frac{\sin(5x)}{2x}$ the angle is $5x$. Make that same quantity appear in the denominator and track the constant needed to do so.

squeeze.example: Near $1$, the bounds $5-(x-1)^2$ and $5+(x-1)^2$ both approach $5$. Any graph lying between them must approach that height.

figure.alt: Two dashed parabolas labeled 5 plus or minus the square of x minus 1 meet at (1, 5).
figure.prompt: A graph stays between these two parabolas near $x=1$. What limit must it have there?
figure.reasoning: Both bounding functions approach $5$ at $1$. By the squeeze theorem, the middle function also has limit $5$.

continuity.title: Continuity
continuity.definition: A function is continuous at $a$ when its value is defined, its finite limit exists, and the two values agree.
continuity.idea: When a graph passes through the height its branches approach, substitution finds the limit immediately. At a piecewise join, compare the branches first.

parts.title: Check the value and the limit
parts.definition: Find the point value, compute the limit, and compare them.
parts.idea: At $-\tfrac12$, read the assigned value from the equality case. Factor the other formula to see what height the rest of the graph approaches.

parts.title: One-sided continuity
parts.definition: A function is right-continuous at $a$ when its right-hand limit equals its value there. Left-continuity uses the left-hand limit.
parts.idea: The square-root graph starts at $0$. Only inputs in its domain can approach that endpoint, so trace the branch from the right.

parts.title: Continuity on an interval
parts.definition: A function is continuous on an interval if it is continuous at every interior point, right-continuous at an included left endpoint, and left-continuous at an included right endpoint.
parts.idea: For $\sqrt{x}$ on $[0,\infty)$, the continuity check at $0$ uses inputs from the right. Every point farther along that interval has inputs on both sides.

parts.title: Choosing constants for continuity
parts.definition: At an interior joining point, set the two one-sided limits equal to the assigned value.
parts.idea: Write down the left height, the height of the filled point, and the right height separately. Equating those three numbers gives equations for the unknown constants.

parts.title: Operations and composition
parts.definition: Sums, products, quotients, powers, and roots of continuous functions are continuous wherever defined. If $g(x)\to L$ and $F$ is continuous at $L$, pass the limit through $F$ wherever the composition is defined near $a$.
parts.idea: Work through the formula from the inside out. If $g(x)$ approaches $-1$, check the outer function at $-1$ before putting that value into it.

continuity.example: In Example 1, $f(-\frac12)=-3$ but the limit is $-\frac72$. The graph has a break at $-\frac12$.

ivt.title: Intermediate Value Theorem
ivt.definition: Suppose $f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$. For every $N$ between $f(a)$ and $f(b)$, some input $c$ in the interval satisfies $f(c)=N$.
ivt.idea: If the endpoint heights lie on opposite sides of a chosen horizontal line, a continuous graph has to cross it somewhere. This can settle an existence question even when the equation is difficult to solve.

parts.title: Does the equation have a solution?
parts.definition: If a continuous function has endpoint values of opposite signs, it has a zero between the endpoints.
parts.idea: Sketch the horizontal axis and mark the signs of the polynomial at $0$ and $2$. What must happen to the graph on its way from one endpoint to the other?
parts.reasoning: The polynomial $f(x)=4x^3-6x^2+3x-2$ is continuous. Since $f(0)=-2<0<12=f(2)$, the IVT gives $f(c)=0$ for some $c\in(0,2)$.

parts.title: Home to campus and back
parts.definition: Follow the morning trip and the return trip along the same path, starting the clock at seven for each.
parts.idea: Imagine starting both trips at the same time and comparing the travelers’ positions minute by minute. What happens to their order during the hour?
parts.reasoning: The difference of the two positions is continuous and has opposite signs at the ends of the hour. The IVT gives a time when the difference is zero, so the travelers are at the same place the same number of minutes after seven.

ivt.example: In class, the polynomial $4x^3-6x^2+3x-2$ changes sign between $0$ and $2$. Its graph must meet the horizontal axis in that interval.

figure.alt: A horizontal line at height N lies between the endpoint heights. It intersects the continuous graph above an input marked c.
figure.prompt: For a continuous function on $[a,b]$, why must the graph reach a height $N$ between $f(a)$ and $f(b)$?
figure.reasoning: The Intermediate Value Theorem gives an input $c\in[a,b]$ with $f(c)=N$. On the diagram, the line at height $N$ meets the curve above $c$.

evt.title: Extreme Value Theorem
evt.definition: A continuous function on a closed interval $[a,b]$ attains a global minimum $m$ and a global maximum $M$. The values occur at inputs $u,v$ in the interval.
evt.idea: Before hunting for a highest or lowest point, check whether the domain includes both ends and the function is continuous throughout. Then the search is guaranteed to succeed.
evt.example: For $f(x)=x^3(4-x)$ on $[-1,4]$, the lowest value is $f(-1)=-5$ and the highest is $f(3)=27$.

parts.title: The domain matters
parts.definition: Compare the same function $q(x)=(x-1)^2$ on $[0,2]$ and on $(0,2)$.
parts.idea: Removing an endpoint can remove the only place a height was reached. A graph can still get arbitrarily close to that height.
parts.reasoning: For $q(x)=(x-1)^2$ on $[0,2]$, the minimum is $0$ at $1$ and the maximum is $1$ at both endpoints. On $(0,2)$, the minimum stays $0$ and there is no maximum.

parts.title: Which values are attained?
parts.definition: There are $u,v\in[a,b]$ for which $f(u)=m$ and $f(v)=M$. The Intermediate Value Theorem gives every output between $m$ and $M$.
parts.idea: First locate where the lowest and highest outputs occur. On the interval between those two inputs, continuity forces the graph to pass through every height in between.

endbehavior.title: End behavior and asymptotes
endbehavior.definition: End behavior describes what happens to $f(x)$ as $x$ increases or decreases without bound.
endbehavior.idea: A graph can keep rising and still get closer to a line. To see which line its tail follows, look at the vertical distance between the curve and the proposed line.
endbehavior.example: For $f(x)=\frac{x^2-1}{x}$, the graph follows $y=x$ because $f(x)-x=-\frac1x\to0$ at both ends.

parts.title: Limit at infinity
parts.definition: We write $\lim_{x\to+\infty}f(x)=L$ when $f(x)$ approaches $L$ as $x$ increases without bound. At $-\infty$, follow $x$ as it decreases without bound.
parts.idea: Follow each tail of the graph separately. The right tail and the left tail can approach different heights.
parts.reasoning: At $+\infty$, for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is an $M$ such that $|f(x)-L|<\varepsilon$ at all domain points $x>M$, with the domain unbounded above. At $-\infty$, use a domain unbounded below and $x<M$.

parts.title: Horizontal asymptote
parts.definition: The line $y=L$ is a horizontal asymptote if $f(x)$ tends to $L$ at either end.
parts.idea: A tail can cross the same horizontal line many times. What matters is whether the distance to that line shrinks as you follow the tail farther out.

parts.title: Slant asymptote
parts.definition: A line $y=mx+b$ with $m\ne0$ is a slant asymptote if the difference between the function and the line tends to zero at either end.
parts.idea: Subtract the proposed line from the function. This removes the part that grows along the line and leaves just the vertical difference.

figure.alt: A curve and an oblique line with the vertical distance between them marked at one input.
figure.prompt: For $f(x)=\frac{x^2-1}{x}$, what line does the curve approach at each end? Use the vertical difference to justify your answer.
figure.reasoning: Write $f(x)=x-\frac1x$. The difference from $y=x$ is $-\frac1x$, which tends to $0$ at both ends.

parts.title: Two different horizontal asymptotes
parts.definition: Find both end limits of $f(x)=\frac{\sqrt{4x^2+1}}{x}$.
parts.idea: Pulling $x^2$ out of a square root gives $|x|$. The factor $|x|/x$ changes sign between the two tails, so the same formula can approach two different heights.
parts.reasoning: For $f(x)=\frac{\sqrt{4x^2+1}}{x}$, the right-hand tail approaches $y=2$ and the left-hand tail approaches $y=-2$.

lhospital.title: l’Hospital’s rule
lhospital.definition: Suppose $f$ and $g$ are differentiable near $a$, except possibly at $a$, with $g'(x)\ne0$ there for $x\ne a$. For a quotient of form $0/0$ or $\infty/\infty$, use the following equality if the limit on the right exists, finite or infinite.
lhospital.idea: Both $e^x$ and $x^2$ grow without bound. Their quotient asks which grows faster. Here, differentiating twice leaves an exponential over a constant, so the comparison is visible.

parts.title: Indeterminate form
parts.definition: A quotient has form $0/0$ when its numerator and denominator both tend to zero. It has form $\infty/\infty$ when both grow without bound in magnitude.
parts.idea: As $x\to0$, the numerators and denominators of $x/x$ and $x^2/x$ all tend to zero. The quotients approach $1$ and $0$, so knowing the form alone leaves the answer open.

parts.title: Check the form
parts.definition: Find the numerator and denominator limits separately. l’Hospital’s rule requires $0/0$ or $\infty/\infty$.
parts.idea: Test the rule against $\frac{x^2}{x}$ at $1$. The ordinary quotient law applies immediately, and differentiating the two parts would give the wrong limit.

parts.title: Zero over zero
parts.definition: When both parts of a quotient tend to zero and the theorem applies, differentiate the numerator and denominator separately.
parts.idea: The hole in $\frac{x^2-4}{x-2}$ was one of the first limit examples. Check the two separate limits at $2$, then compare this new method with factoring.
parts.reasoning: At $2$ the quotient has form $0/0$. The derivative quotient is $2x$, so the limit is $4$.

parts.title: Infinity over infinity
parts.definition: The rule also applies when both the numerator and denominator grow without bound in magnitude and the derivative quotient has a limit.
parts.idea: For $\frac{e^x}{x^2}$, follow what happens to the denominator after each differentiation. Check the form again before taking the next step.
parts.reasoning: The first derivative quotient is $\frac{e^x}{2x}$, again of form $\infty/\infty$. The second is $\frac{e^x}{2}$, whose limit is $+\infty$.

lhospital.example: How much faster does $e^x$ grow than $x^2$? Applying the rule twice gives $\lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{e^x}{x^2}=+\infty$.

derivative.title: Derivative at a point
derivative.definition: The derivative of $f$ at $a$ is the limit of the difference quotient, provided the limit exists as a finite number. We say $f$ is differentiable at $a$ when this derivative exists.
derivative.idea: One point gives a position but no slope. Bring a second point toward it to see whether slopes measured over shorter and shorter intervals settle on one value.
derivative.example: For $f(x)=3x-x^2$ at $x=1$, the secant slopes approach $1$.

parts.title: Difference quotient
parts.definition: The secant line passes through $(a,f(a))$ and $(a+h,f(a+h))$, where $h\ne0$. Its slope is the difference quotient, the average rate of change of $f$ between the two inputs.
parts.idea: First measure change over a nonzero interval. Setting $h=0$ would make the two points coincide before there is a slope to measure.
parts.aliases: average rate of change difference quotient

figure.alt: A parabola passes through P at (1,2) and a second point Q. A secant joins P to Q, and a tangent passes through P.
figure.prompt: On $y=3x-x^2$, keep $P=(1,2)$ fixed and move $Q$ toward it. What slope do the secants approach?
figure.reasoning: For $x\ne1$, the secant slope is $\frac{3x-x^2-2}{x-1}=2-x$. As $x\to1$, it approaches $1$.

parts.title: Computing a derivative from the definition
parts.definition: For $f(x)=\sqrt{x+5}$, find the tangent slope at $x=4$.
parts.idea: The radical gives $0/0$ at $x=4$. Multiplying by its conjugate exposes a factor of $x-4$ that cancels at the nearby inputs used by the limit.
parts.reasoning: For $f(x)=\sqrt{x+5}$, the quotient becomes $\frac{1}{\sqrt{x+5}+3}$ for $x\ne4$. Thus $f'(4)=\frac16$.

figure.alt: A tangent of slope one sixth meets the square-root graph at (4,3).
figure.prompt: Use the definition of the derivative to find the tangent slope of $y=\sqrt{x+5}$ at $x=4$.
figure.reasoning: Multiplying by the conjugate gives $\frac{\sqrt{x+5}-3}{x-4}=\frac1{\sqrt{x+5}+3}$ for $x\ne4$. The limit is $\frac16$.

parts.title: When the derivative does not exist
parts.definition: A derivative at a point exists when the left- and right-hand difference quotients approach the same finite number.
parts.idea: A tangent gives one slope at a point. Approach from each side and check whether both sides give that slope.

figure.alt: The two straight sides of the V meet at the origin. The left side is labeled slope −1 and the right side slope 1.
figure.prompt: Does $f(x)=|x|$ have a tangent slope at $x=0$? Compare the slopes from the two sides.
figure.reasoning: The difference quotient is $\frac{|h|}{h}$. It equals $-1$ for $h<0$ and $1$ for $h>0$, so $f'(0)$ does not exist.

derivative2.title: Derivative function
derivative2.definition: The derivative function assigns a tangent slope to each input where the difference quotient has a finite limit.
derivative2.idea: A graph of $f'$ turns steepness into height. A nearly horizontal stretch of $f$ appears near the horizontal axis of the derivative graph, even if $f$ itself is high above it.

parts.title: Finding the derivative function
parts.definition: For $f(x)=3x-x^2$, use the difference quotient with $x$ left as a variable.
parts.idea: Keep the starting input $x$ fixed while the second input $x+h$ moves toward it. Leaving $x$ as a letter gives all the slopes in one calculation.
parts.reasoning: For $f(x)=3x-x^2$, the difference quotient simplifies to $3-2x-h$. Thus $f'(x)=3-2x$ and $f'(1)=1$.

parts.title: Higher-order derivatives
parts.definition: Differentiate $f'$ to get the second derivative $f''$. Repeating this process gives the third derivative and, in general, the $n$th derivative where it exists.
parts.idea: For the parabola $3x-x^2$, the tangent slope drops by two each time $x$ increases by one. The second derivative records that steady change in slope.

parts.title: Prime and Leibniz notation
parts.definition: Prime notation and Leibniz notation give two ways to write the same derivative.
parts.idea: In $\left.\frac{df}{dx}\right|_{x=a}$, the order matters. Keep $x$ variable while differentiating, then use $a$ to find one particular slope.

parts.title: Differentiability implies continuity
parts.definition: If $f'(a)$ exists, then $f$ is continuous at $a$.
parts.idea: Check continuity first when a graph has a hole or a jump. At a point where the graph does join, a corner can still give two different one-sided slopes.

parts.title: Reading the derivative graph
parts.definition: The height of the graph of $f'$ gives the tangent slope of $f$ at the same input.
parts.idea: Ask two questions about $f'$. Its height tells whether $f$ rises or falls. The slope of $f'$ tells whether the tangent slopes of $f$ are increasing or decreasing.

figure.alt: The graph of f prime passes through (−4,2), (−2,−2), (0,2), (2,−2), and (4,2) with smooth turns. It crosses the horizontal axis at −3, −1, 1, and 3.
figure.prompt: The curve shows $y=f'(x)$ on $(-4,4)$. Where is $f$ decreasing? Where does it have horizontal tangents? What happens at $x=2$?
figure.reasoning: The graph lies below the axis on $(-3,-1)$ and $(1,3)$, so $f$ decreases there. The zeros at $-3,-1,1,3$ give horizontal tangents to $f$. At $x=2$, the tangent to $f$ has slope $f'(2)=-2$.

tangent.title: Tangent line
tangent.definition: At a point of differentiability, the tangent line passes through $(a,f(a))$ and has slope $f'(a)$. This slope is the instantaneous rate of change of $f$ at $a$.
tangent.idea: Close to a point of differentiability, following the tangent line gives a simple estimate of the new height. A small horizontal move $\Delta x$ produces a vertical move of about $f'(a)\Delta x$.
tangent.example: For $f(x)=\frac3{x^2}+1$ at $x=1$, the tangent line is $y-4=-6(x-1)$.

parts.title: Point-slope form
parts.definition: To find a tangent line at $x=a$, compute the point $(a,f(a))$ and the slope $f'(a)$.
parts.idea: Use $f(a)$ to place the line and $f'(a)$ to tilt it. The expression $x-a$ measures how far you have moved from the point where both were found.
parts.reasoning: At $x=1$ on $f(x)=3/x^2+1$, the height is $4$ and the slope is $-6$. The line is $y-4=-6(x-1)$.

parts.title: Prescribed slopes
parts.definition: To find the points with a given tangent slope $m$, solve for the inputs and evaluate $f$ at each one.
parts.idea: Here the slope is given and the point is missing. Solve an equation for the slope first, then return to the original function to recover the heights.
parts.reasoning: For $f(x)=x^3-3x^2+2$, the horizontal tangents occur at $(0,2)$ and $(2,-2)$.

parts.title: Zooming in at a point
parts.definition: Near a point of differentiability, the tangent line gives a linear approximation to the curve.
parts.idea: Keep the point of contact in view as you zoom. A curved graph and its tangent may separate farther away, yet be difficult to distinguish near that point.
parts.reasoning: Zoom in at $(a,f(a))$. The curve looks almost straight, and the slope of that line is the derivative.

figure.alt: Two views show a smooth curve and its tangent at a marked point. After magnification, the two lines almost coincide near the point.
figure.prompt: When you zoom in near $x=a$, how can the tangent slope predict the change in $f$ over a small input change $h$?
figure.reasoning: The tangent changes by $f'(a)h$. Near $a$, the curve follows the tangent closely, so $f(a+h)-f(a)\approx f'(a)h$.

motion.title: Motion
motion.definition: Velocity is the derivative of position with respect to time. Acceleration is the derivative of velocity.
motion.idea: A velocity that changes from $-2$ to $-5$ means the particle is moving faster in the negative direction. Position, direction, and speed answer different questions about the same motion.
motion.example: For $s(t)=3t-t^2$, the velocity is $3-2t$ and the acceleration is $-2$. At $t=\frac32$ the particle reverses direction.

parts.title: Average and instantaneous velocity
parts.definition: Average velocity is the change in position divided by elapsed time. Its limit over shorter intervals gives instantaneous velocity.
parts.idea: A trip can end where it began even if the particle moved the whole time. A shorter time interval can reveal motion that the average over the full trip hides.

parts.title: Direction and speed
parts.definition: The sign of velocity gives direction. Speed is the absolute value of velocity.
parts.idea: Velocity keeps track of which way the particle moves. Speed lets you compare how fast two particles move even when they travel in opposite directions.

figure.alt: The position curve rises until time 3/2 and then falls. The velocity sign chart changes from positive to negative there, and acceleration stays negative.
figure.prompt: For $s(t)=3t-t^2$ on $[0,3]$, when does the particle reverse direction?
figure.reasoning: Velocity is $v(t)=3-2t$. It is positive before $t=\frac32$ and negative afterward, so the particle reverses at $t=\frac32$.

parts.reasoning: For $s(t)=3t-t^2$ on $[0,3]$, velocity changes from positive to negative at $t=\frac32$, where the particle turns around.

parts.title: Speeding up and slowing down
parts.definition: Make sign graphs for velocity and acceleration. Matching signs mean the speed increases, and opposite signs mean it decreases.
parts.idea: Place the velocity and acceleration sign graphs above one another. On an interval where both are negative, the velocity moves farther below zero, so its magnitude increases.

parts.title: Read the event before substituting
parts.definition: At the origin, position is zero. At rest, velocity is zero. At impact with the ground, height is zero.
parts.idea: The input to $v(t)$ is a time. A phrase such as “when the ball hits the ground” gives a height condition that you can solve to find that time.
parts.example: For $H(t)=96-16t-16t^2$, impact occurs at $t=2$ seconds. The velocity is $-80$ ft/s and the speed is $80$ ft/s.
parts.reasoning: For $H(t)=96-16t-16t^2$, impact occurs at $t=2$ seconds. Just before impact the velocity is $-80$ ft/s and the speed is $80$ ft/s.

parts.title: Newton’s law of motion
parts.definition: For an object of constant mass on a line, force equals mass times acceleration.
parts.idea: For a fixed mass, the force tells how quickly velocity is changing. This makes it possible to say something about motion even when a formula for position is unknown.
parts.reasoning: A law about forces becomes a differential equation for the position $x(t)$.

rules.title: Differentiation rules
rules.definition: The differentiation rules give the derivative of a sum, difference, constant multiple, power, product, or quotient on its domain of differentiability.
rules.idea: The same function can offer two routes. Expand $x(3-x)$ and use the sum and power rules, or leave it factored and use the product rule. The slopes must agree.

parts.title: Sums and constant multiples
parts.definition: Differentiate each term and carry its constant factor. The derivative of a constant is zero.
parts.idea: Adding a constant shifts a graph vertically while keeping its slopes. Multiplying the heights by a constant multiplies the slopes by that same constant.
parts.reasoning: For $p(x)=4x^3-2x+7$, the derivative is $p'(x)=12x^2-2$.

parts.title: Power rule
parts.definition: For a constant exponent $n$, the power rule holds for $x>0$ and wherever both sides are defined for other inputs. For $n=0$, use the constant rule.
parts.idea: A reciprocal can already be a power problem. Rewriting $3/x$ as $3x^{-1}$ makes the exponent visible and preserves the restriction $x\ne0$.

parts.title: Product rule
parts.definition: Differentiate one factor at a time and add the two terms.
parts.idea: Both factors can contribute to the change in a product. Hold one at its current value while accounting for the change in the other, then switch their roles.

figure.alt: A rectangle of area uv grows along two edges. Two added strips have areas v times the change in u and u times the change in v. The small corner has area equal to the product of the changes.
figure.prompt: Divide the change in area by the input change $h$. Which pieces of the rectangle contribute to the product rule as $h$ approaches zero?
figure.reasoning: The strips contribute $vu'$ and $uv'$. The corner contributes $\Delta u\cdot\frac{\Delta v}{h}$, which tends to zero since $\Delta u\to0$ and $\frac{\Delta v}{h}\to v'$.

parts.example: For $f(x)=x(3-x)$, the two terms are $3-x$ and $-x$. Thus $f'(x)=3-2x$.

parts.title: Quotient rule
parts.definition: For differentiable $f$ and $g$ with $g(x)\ne0$, keep the original denominator when forming the first term of the numerator.
parts.idea: For positive quantities, increasing the numerator raises the quotient, while increasing the denominator lowers it. Those two contributions explain the subtraction and why its order matters.

chain.title: Chain rule
chain.definition: If $g$ is differentiable at $a$ and $f$ is differentiable at $g(a)$, then the composition $f\circ g$ is differentiable at $a$.
chain.idea: A step in $x$ changes the inner value first. The outer function responds to that change, which is why the two local rates multiply.
chain.example: For $y=(\cos x)^4$, this gives $y'=-4\cos^3 x\sin x$.

parts.title: Inner and outer functions
parts.definition: Write $F(x)=f(g(x))$. The inner function $g$ supplies the input to the outer function $f$.
parts.idea: Read $\sin(2x)$ from the inside out to identify the functions. Doubling the angle doubles how quickly the input to sine changes.
parts.reasoning: $\frac{d}{dx}\sin(2x)=2\cos(2x)$.

parts.title: Using a table
parts.definition: To find $(f\circ g)'(0)$, look up $g(0)$ before looking up the outer derivative.
parts.idea: One input can lead you to two different rows. First look up the inner value to see where the outer derivative must be evaluated.
parts.reasoning: In the class table, $(f\circ g)'(0)=f'(1)g'(0)=5(-2)=-10$.

parts.title: Powers of functions
parts.definition: Differentiate the outer power and multiply by the derivative of the inside function, wherever both derivatives exist.
parts.idea: Writing $\cos^4x$ as $(\cos x)^4$ makes the outer power visible. After differentiating that power, one factor still has to account for the changing cosine.
parts.reasoning: $\frac{d}{dx}\cos^4x=-4\cos^3x\sin x$.

parts.title: Three or more layers
parts.definition: Apply the chain rule repeatedly, working from the outside inward.
parts.idea: In $[\sin(\cos(2x))]^3$, read inward from the cube through sine, cosine, and $2x$. Crossing off each layer after differentiating it helps keep the last factor of $2$.

implicit.title: Implicit differentiation
implicit.definition: To differentiate an equation relating $x$ and $y$, treat $y$ as a function of $x$. Differentiate both sides and solve for $y'$.
implicit.idea: The equation for a circle describes an upper and a lower branch at once. Differentiating the equation lets the coordinates of the chosen point determine its slope.

parts.title: Explicit and implicit equations
parts.definition: An explicit formula gives $y$ as a function of $x$. An implicit equation relates $x$ and $y$ and may describe several branches.
parts.idea: At $x=0$ the circle $x^2+y^2=1$ contains both $(0,1)$ and $(0,-1)$. Solving explicitly requires choosing the upper or lower branch.

parts.title: Differentiate both sides
parts.definition: Treat $y$ as a function of $x$. Use the chain rule wherever $y$ appears, then collect the terms containing $y'$.
parts.idea: Along the circle, a change in $x^2$ must be balanced by a change in $y^2$. The factor $y'$ tells how much $y$ changes as $x$ moves.
parts.reasoning: For $x^2+y^2=1$, $2x+2yy'=0$. Where $y\ne0$, $y'=-x/y$, giving slope $-1$ at $(1/\sqrt2,1/\sqrt2)$.

parts.title: Finding a tangent slope
parts.definition: On $x^2+xy+y^2=13$, use the product rule on $xy$ and the chain rule on $y^2$.
parts.idea: In $xy$, both factors change along the curve. Keep the two terms from the product rule, then gather all the terms containing $y'$ before substituting the point.

parts.title: Horizontal tangents
parts.definition: A horizontal tangent has $\frac{dy}{dx}=0$. On $x^2+xy+y^2=3$, this requires $2x+y=0$ and $x+2y\ne0$.
parts.idea: A slope of zero singles out possible inputs and outputs. Keep only pairs that also satisfy the original curve equation and give a nonzero denominator.
parts.reasoning: On $x^2+xy+y^2=3$, substituting $y=-2x$ gives the points $(1,-2)$ and $(-1,2)$.

parts.title: Vertical tangents
parts.definition: To find vertical tangents on $x^2+xy+y^2=3$, differentiate with respect to $y$ and solve $\frac{dx}{dy}=0$.
parts.idea: Exchange the roles of the coordinates. At a vertical tangent, the horizontal change per unit vertical change is zero, so $\frac{dx}{dy}$ is the easier slope to study.

figure.alt: The tilted ellipse has vertical tangents at (−2,1) and (2,−1) and horizontal tangents at (−1,2) and (1,−2).
figure.prompt: Where does the ellipse $x^2+xy+y^2=3$ have vertical tangents?
figure.reasoning: Set $\frac{dx}{dy}=-\frac{x+2y}{2x+y}=0$. Substituting $x=-2y$ into the ellipse gives $3y^2=3$. Both $(-2,1)$ and $(2,-1)$ have $2x+y\ne0$.

parts.reasoning: On $x^2+xy+y^2=3$, set $x=-2y$ in the original equation. The points are $(-2,1)$ and $(2,-1)$, with $2x+y\ne0$ at both.

rates.title: Related rates
rates.definition: In a related rates problem, one rate is given and another is sought at the same instant. An equation relates the changing quantities.
rates.idea: Two measurements can change at different rates even though they describe one moving object. An equation that holds throughout its motion links those rates at the instant in question.
rates.example: On $y=x^2$, when $x=3$ and $\frac{dx}{dt}=2$, the rate $\frac{dy}{dt}$ is $12$.

parts.title: Understand the situation
parts.definition: Label the changing quantities, record the given rate, and identify the rate to find.
parts.idea: Give each changing measurement its own name. The sketch then shows what is measured at the given instant and which rate is still unknown.
parts.reasoning: On $y=x^2$, the given instant has $x=3$ and $\frac{dx}{dt}=2$. The requested rate is $\frac{dy}{dt}$.

parts.title: Relate rates
parts.definition: Write an equation relating the quantities, then differentiate with respect to time.
parts.idea: A quantity with no explicit time in its formula may still change with time. Writing $x(t)$ makes clear why differentiating its square produces a factor of $\frac{dx}{dt}$.

parts.title: Plug in
parts.definition: Substitute the given values and rate into the differentiated equation at the specified instant.
parts.idea: A measurement at one instant need not be constant. Replacing $x$ with $3$ before differentiating $x^2$ would erase the very change you want to measure.
parts.reasoning: On $y=x^2$, substituting $x=3$ and $\frac{dx}{dt}=2$ after differentiating gives $\frac{dy}{dt}=2(3)(2)=12$.

parts.title: Similar triangles
parts.definition: Suppose two triangles have equal corresponding angles and corresponding side lengths $a,b,c$ and $A,B,C$. The ratios of corresponding sides are equal.
parts.idea: In the conical tank, the water and the tank share the same sloping wall. Their matching triangles turn the changing water radius into a multiple of the depth, leaving one changing length in the volume formula.
parts.reasoning: The tank is 6 m tall with radius 2 m, so $r/h=2/6$ and $r=h/3$.

figure.alt: An inverted tank has height 6 m and top radius 2 m. Inside it, the shaded water has depth h and surface radius r, measured from the same center line.
figure.prompt: Water enters the pictured tank at $\pi\,\mathrm{m^3/min}$. How can you use similar triangles to find how fast the water level rises when it is 3 m deep?
figure.reasoning: The triangles give $\frac rh=\frac26$, so $V=\frac13\pi r^2h=\frac{\pi h^3}{27}$. Hence $\frac{dV}{dt}=\frac{\pi h^2}{9}\frac{dh}{dt}$. At $h=3$, the water rises at $1\,\mathrm{m/min}$.

inverse.title: Inverse functions
inverse.definition: An inverse function undoes a one-to-one function. Its domain is the range of the original function.
inverse.idea: An output can tell you which input produced it only when that output was used once. On the graph, following a horizontal line back to the curve makes this visible.

parts.title: One-to-one and domain restrictions
parts.definition: A function is one-to-one if each output comes from only one input.
parts.idea: Both $2$ and $-2$ square to $4$. Choosing a side of the parabola decides which of those two inputs the inverse should return.
parts.reasoning: On $x\ge0$, the inverse of $x^2$ is $\sqrt{x}$.

parts.title: The graph of an inverse
parts.definition: A point on the graph of $f$ gives a point on the graph of $f^{-1}$ by exchanging its coordinates.
parts.idea: Reflection across $y=x$ exchanges rise and run. A steep nonhorizontal tangent on one graph therefore becomes a shallow tangent on the other.

figure.alt: A curve and its reflection across y = x have tangents at the corresponding points (a,b) and (b,a).
figure.prompt: Suppose $f$ satisfies the inverse-function derivative theorem, $f(2)=5$, and $f'(2)=-3$. Where is the corresponding point on the inverse graph, and what is its tangent slope?
figure.reasoning: Exchanging the coordinates gives $(5,2)$. Reflection exchanges rise and run, so $(f^{-1})'(5)=\frac1{f'(2)}=-\frac13$.

parts.title: The inverse-function derivative
parts.definition: Suppose $f$ is continuous and one-to-one on an open interval containing $a$, differentiable at $a$, and $f'(a)\ne0$. Set $b=f(a)$.
parts.idea: To find the inverse slope at $5$, ask which original input maps to $5$. The slope to invert belongs to that input.
parts.reasoning: If $f(2)=5$ and $f'(2)=-3$, the inverse slope at $5$ is $-1/3$ under the theorem’s hypotheses.

exp.title: Exponentials and logarithms
exp.definition: The derivative of the natural exponential equals the exponential itself. Its inverse, the natural logarithm, has derivative $1/x$ for $x>0$.
exp.idea: On $y=e^x$, the height of the graph at a point already tells you its slope. Reading that same graph with the coordinates exchanged gives the slope of the logarithm.
exp.example: At $(0,1)$ on $y=e^x$, the tangent slope is $1$ and the tangent line is $y=1+x$.

parts.title: Exponential and logarithmic functions
parts.definition: For $a>0$ and $a\ne1$, $x\mapsto a^x$ takes $\mathbb R$ onto $(0,\infty)$. Its inverse, $\log_a$, takes $(0,\infty)$ onto $\mathbb R$. The base $a=1$ gives the constant function $1$.
parts.idea: The logarithm returns the exponent. For example, $2^3=8$ gives $\log_2 8=3$; the two graphs exchange the coordinates $(3,8)$ and $(8,3)$.

figure.alt: An increasing exponential and its logarithmic inverse reflected across the line y=x.

parts.title: The number e
parts.definition: For $a>0$, let $F(a)$ denote the slope of $y=a^x$ at $x=0$. The number $e$ is the base for which that slope is one.
parts.idea: All the graphs $y=a^x$ pass through $(0,1)$. Vary the base and watch the tangent there turn. The choice $a=e$ gives it slope one.

parts.title: The natural exponential and logarithm
parts.definition: The natural logarithm $\ln x=\log_e x$ is the inverse of $e^x$. Thus $e^{\ln x}=x$ for $x>0$ and $\ln(e^x)=x$ for every real $x$.
parts.idea: In $e^{x^2}$ the exponential grows with its input, but that input moves at rate $2x$. At $x=0$ this makes the tangent horizontal even though an ordinary exponential has positive slope everywhere.

parts.title: Relative growth
parts.definition: Relative growth is the rate of change divided by the current amount. For $P(t)=P_0e^{kt}$ with $P_0>0$, it is constant.
parts.idea: A rate of ten units per hour can be large or small depending on the amount present. Dividing by the current amount lets you compare growth on the same scale.

parts.title: Other bases
parts.definition: For $a>0$, differentiating $a^x$ contributes a factor $\ln a$. For $\log_a x$, also require $a\ne1$ and $x>0$.
parts.idea: Changing the base changes the slope at $(0,1)$. The factor $\ln a$ carries that change into the exponential derivative, and its reciprocal appears when the graph is inverted.

parts.title: Logarithm laws
parts.definition: For positive $u,v$, a logarithm turns a product into a sum, a quotient into a difference, and a power into a multiple.
parts.idea: Look for a product with several changing factors or a power whose exponent changes. Taking the logarithm rewrites these as a sum or a simpler product before differentiation.

figure.alt: The exponential graph has a tangent of slope 1 at (0,1) and another with slope equal to its height at (a,e to the a).
figure.prompt: What is the equation of the tangent to $y=e^x$ at $x=0$?
figure.reasoning: At $x=0$, the height and slope both equal $e^0=1$. The tangent through $(0,1)$ is $y=1+x$.

logdiff.title: Logarithmic differentiation
logdiff.definition: For $y>0$, take the logarithm of both sides, differentiate implicitly, and solve for $y'$.
logdiff.idea: In $x^x$, changing $x$ changes both the base and the exponent. Taking a logarithm puts those two appearances of $x$ into a product where the two changes can be counted separately.
logdiff.example: For $y=x^x$ with $x>0$, the result is $y'=x^x(\ln x+1)$.

parts.title: Taking logarithms
parts.definition: Let $y=x^x$ for $x>0$. Taking logarithms gives $\ln y=x\ln x$.
parts.idea: The derivative of $\ln y$ gives the relative rate $y'/y$. Multiplying by the original $y$ at the end converts it back to the rate the question asks for.
parts.reasoning: For $y=x^x$ with $x>0$, $\ln y=x\ln x$, so $y'/y=\ln x+1$ and $y'=x^x(\ln x+1)$.

parts.title: Variable base and exponent
parts.definition: Suppose $f$ and $g$ are differentiable and $f(x)>0$. For $y=f(x)^{g(x)}$, first write $\ln y=g(x)\ln f(x)$.
parts.idea: One term records how the exponent changes while the base is fixed. The other records how the base changes while the exponent is fixed. If either is constant, its contribution disappears.

parts.title: The power rule for real exponents
parts.definition: For a constant real exponent $r$ and $x>0$, logarithmic differentiation gives the power rule.
parts.idea: A repeated product explains positive integer powers. For $x>0$, taking the logarithm of $x^r$ leaves the exponent as an ordinary constant factor, even when $r$ is fractional or irrational.

trig.title: Trigonometric derivatives
trig.definition: With angles measured in radians, the six trigonometric derivative formulas apply on the domain of each function.
trig.idea: Start with sine and cosine. The other four functions can be written as quotients of the first two, so their derivative formulas can be recovered if a sign slips from memory.
trig.example: A mass on a spring with position $s(t)=\cos t$ has velocity $v(t)=-\sin t$ and acceleration $a(t)=-\cos t$.

parts.title: Sine and cosine
parts.definition: With angles measured in radians, the derivative of sine is cosine, and the derivative of cosine is negative sine.
parts.idea: At the end of its swing, a mass on a spring pauses before reversing direction. The position graph is then at a peak or valley while the velocity graph crosses zero.
parts.reasoning: For $s(t)=\cos t$, $v(t)=-\sin t$ and $a(t)=-\cos t$.

parts.title: Tangent and cotangent
parts.definition: On their domains, tangent differentiates to secant squared and cotangent to negative cosecant squared.
parts.idea: In the derivative of $\sin x/\cos x$, the two numerator terms add to one by the Pythagorean identity. That is why the final formula for tangent is so short.

parts.title: Secant and cosecant
parts.definition: Secant and cosecant are the reciprocals of cosine and sine, respectively. Their derivatives hold wherever the functions are defined.
parts.formula:
$\frac{d}{dx}\sec x=\sec x\tan x$
$\frac{d}{dx}\csc x=-\csc x\cot x$
parts.idea: Write secant as a reciprocal of cosine. The minus sign from differentiating a reciprocal cancels the minus sign from differentiating cosine. Cosecant has only the first minus sign.

parts.title: Choose the rule from the structure
parts.definition: Identify the outer operation before differentiating a trigonometric expression.
parts.idea: In $x^3\cot x$, the multiplication sits outside the trigonometric function. Write the two product-rule terms first, then insert the derivative of cotangent.
parts.reasoning: $\frac{d}{dx}(x^3\cot x)=3x^2\cot x-x^3\csc^2x$.

derivatives.title: Second derivative
derivatives.definition: The derivative of $f'$ is $f''$, read “$f$ double prime.”
derivatives.idea: Imagine walking along a curve and watching the slope of your tangent line. The second derivative tells how quickly that slope changes as you move to the right.

parts.title: Differentiate again
parts.definition: Use the derivative definition with $f'$ in place of $f$.
parts.idea: Use the slope as the new output in the difference quotient. In the lecture parabola, each unit step to the right lowers the slope by two.
parts.reasoning: For $f(x)=3x-x^2$, $f'(x)=3-2x$. The change in slope over a step $h$ is $-2h$, so $f''(x)=-2$.

figure.alt: A horizontal line below the horizontal axis represents the constant second derivative of the parabola.
figure.prompt: For $f(x)=3x-x^2$, sketch $f''$. How does the tangent slope change as $x$ increases by one?
figure.reasoning: Since $f'(x)=3-2x$, the slope falls by $2$ for every unit increase in $x$. Thus $f''(x)=-2$.

parts.title: At a horizontal tangent
parts.definition: Suppose $f'(c)=0$ and $f''$ is continuous near $c$. A positive second derivative at $c$ gives a local minimum, and a negative one gives a local maximum.
parts.idea: If the slopes are increasing through zero, the graph falls into the point and then rises away from it. Decreasing slopes through zero give the opposite picture.
parts.reasoning: For $f(x)=x\tan x$, $f'(0)=0$ and $f''(0)=2$. The graph has a strict local minimum at $(0,0)$.

monotonic.title: Increasing and decreasing
monotonic.definition: On an interval, $f$ increases when larger inputs give larger outputs. It decreases when larger inputs give smaller outputs.
monotonic.idea: The sign of the slope tells which way to draw each branch as you move from left to right. You can find the intervals of increase and decrease before sketching the curve.
monotonic.example: For $f(x)=4x^3-12x+12$ on $[-2,3]$, the derivative has signs $+,-,+$ on the intervals cut by $-1$ and $1$.

parts.title: The sign of the derivative
parts.definition: A positive derivative throughout an interval implies increase there. A negative derivative throughout the interval implies decrease.
parts.idea: Picture two inputs in the same interval. When every tangent slopes upward between them, the graph reaches the second input at a greater height.
parts.aliases: MVT Mean Value Theorem increasing decreasing

parts.title: Drawing a sign graph
parts.definition: Mark the breaks in the domain, the zeros of $f'$, and the inputs where $f'$ is undefined. Determine the sign on each intervening interval.
parts.idea: Factor the derivative and mark its zeros and domain breaks first. Between those marks, use the signs of the factors to decide which way the graph moves.
parts.reasoning: For $f'(x)=12(x-1)(x+1)$ on $(-2,3)$, the signs are $+,-,+$ on the intervals cut by $-1$ and $1$.

figure.alt: The sign graph for the derivative has signs positive, negative, positive on the three intervals separated by −1 and 1.
figure.prompt: On $[-2,3]$, draw the sign graph for $f'(x)=12(x-1)(x+1)$. Where is $f$ increasing and where is it decreasing?
figure.reasoning: The factors have the same sign on $(-2,-1)$ and $(1,3)$, so $f$ increases on those intervals. They have opposite signs on $(-1,1)$, where $f$ decreases.

concavity.title: Concavity
concavity.definition: On an interval where $f$ is differentiable, its graph is concave up if $f'$ is increasing and concave down if $f'$ is decreasing.
concavity.idea: A line keeps the same slope. A falling curve can bend upward when its negative tangent slopes grow closer to zero.
concavity.example: For $g(x)=x^3+1$, the slopes $g'(x)=3x^2$ decrease up to $0$ and increase after $0$.

parts.title: Tangent slopes
parts.definition: Compare tangent slopes at two inputs $u<v$ in the interval. Larger slopes farther right give concavity up. Smaller slopes farther right give concavity down.
parts.idea: Read the tangent lines from left to right. If they change from steeply downhill to gently downhill, the graph is still falling while it bends upward.

parts.title: Concavity test
parts.definition: If $f''>0$ throughout an interval, the graph is concave up there. If $f''<0$ throughout the interval, it is concave down.
parts.idea: Think of $f'$ as a graph of slopes. Wherever that graph rises, the tangent lines to $f$ turn upward, even if some of those lines still slope downward.

figure.alt: Two curves with three tangent lines each. From left to right, the slopes increase in the first drawing and decrease in the second.
figure.prompt: How can the tangent lines tell you which way a curve bends?
figure.reasoning: Read the tangent slopes from left to right. Increasing slopes give concavity up, and decreasing slopes give concavity down.

inflect.title: Inflection points
inflect.definition: If $f$ is continuous at $c$ and its graph changes concavity there, then $(c,f(c))$ is an inflection point.
inflect.idea: An inflection point marks where the graph changes the way it bends. A curve can flatten out there and still be rising on both sides.
inflect.example: The graph of $g(x)=x^3+1$ changes from concave down to concave up at $(0,1)$.

parts.title: Where does concavity change?
parts.definition: Make a sign graph for $f''$. Look for adjacent intervals with opposite concavities and verify continuity at their common input.
parts.idea: Use the sign graph of $f''$ to find adjacent intervals that bend in opposite directions. Return to $f$ for the height of the point where the bend changes.
parts.reasoning: For $g(x)=x^3+1$, $g''(x)=6x$ changes from negative to positive at $0$. Since $g(0)=1$, the inflection point is $(0,1)$.

parts.title: A break in the domain
parts.definition: For $f(x)=\frac{x}{x+1}$, the change in concavity occurs across $x=-1$, outside the domain.
parts.idea: Two separate branches can bend in opposite directions. Check that they actually meet at a continuous point before marking an inflection.
parts.reasoning: For $f(x)=\frac{x}{x+1}$ the left branch is concave up and the right branch is concave down. The input $-1$ is excluded, so the graph has no inflection point.

figure.alt: The increasing cubic bends down to the left of zero, flattens at (0,1), and bends up to its right.
figure.prompt: Where does $g(x)=x^3+1$ change concavity? Does the function change direction at that point?
figure.reasoning: $g''(x)=6x$ changes sign at $0$, and $g(0)=1$. The inflection point is $(0,1)$. Since $g'(x)=3x^2>0$ on both sides, the curve keeps increasing.

critical.title: Critical numbers
critical.definition: A critical number is an input $c$ in the domain $D$ of $f$ where $f'(c)=0$ or $f'(c)$ does not exist. Its output $f(c)$ is a critical value.
critical.idea: These are the interior inputs worth checking for a peak or a valley. Once you find a candidate, trace the graph on either side to decide what happens.
critical.example: For $f(x)=2+|x|$, $0$ is a critical number and $f(0)=2$ is the corresponding critical value.

parts.title: A zero derivative
parts.definition: A differentiable function can pass through a horizontal tangent and keep increasing.
parts.idea: A horizontal tangent records the slope at a single input. The graph could turn there or flatten for a moment and continue in the same direction.

figure.alt: The graph of the cubic passes through the origin with a horizontal tangent and keeps increasing.
figure.prompt: For $f(x)=x^3$, is $0$ a critical number? Does $f(0)$ give a local extremum?
figure.reasoning: $f'(0)=0$, so $0$ is critical. The outputs just left of $0$ are negative and those just right are positive. The origin gives neither a local maximum nor a local minimum.

parts.reasoning: For $f(x)=x^3$, $f'(0)=0$ and $f'(x)=3x^2>0$ on both sides of zero. There is no local extremum at $0$.

parts.title: An undefined derivative
parts.definition: For $f(x)=2+|x|$, the left slope at $0$ is $-1$ and the right slope is $1$. The derivative at $0$ does not exist.
parts.idea: At a corner the graph can turn even though it has no single tangent slope. Check any such input that belongs to the domain.
parts.reasoning: For $f(x)=2+|x|$, the slopes are $-1$ on the left of $0$ and $1$ on the right. The minimum value is $f(0)=2$.

parts.title: Critical number and critical value
parts.definition: A critical number is an input. Evaluating the original function there gives its critical value.
parts.idea: Solve using $f'$ to find the inputs, then substitute those inputs into $f$ to find the heights. A sign graph for $f'$ alone gives no numerical height.
parts.reasoning: For $f(x)=x^3(4-x)$ the interior critical numbers are $0$ and $3$ on $[-1,4]$. The corresponding values are $0$ and $27$.

global.title: Global extrema
global.definition: A global maximum is the largest output attained anywhere in the domain $D$. A global minimum is the smallest.
global.idea: The tallest interior peak can still be lower than an endpoint. Compare actual function values across the whole allowed domain.
global.example: For $f(x)=1-x^2$ on $[-1,3]$, the global maximum is $1$ at $x=0$ and the global minimum is $-8$ at $x=3$.

parts.title: Closed-interval method
parts.definition: For a continuous function on $[a,b]$, list both endpoints and every interior critical number. Compare the function values at these inputs.
parts.idea: Continuity guarantees that both extrema occur. Fermat’s theorem narrows the search to the endpoints and the interior critical numbers.

parts.title: Check the endpoints
parts.definition: The function $f(x)=x+2$ on $[-1,1]$ has no interior critical numbers because $f'(x)=1$ throughout.
parts.idea: A function can rise all the way from one end to the other. In that case both extremes occur at the boundary, and solving $f'(x)=0$ finds neither one.
parts.reasoning: For $f(x)=x+2$ on $[-1,1]$, $f'(x)=1$ everywhere. The minimum is $f(-1)=1$ and the maximum is $f(1)=3$.

local.title: Local extrema
local.definition: A local maximum at $c$ means $f(c)$ is at least as large as every nearby output. Reverse the inequality for a local minimum.
local.idea: Imagine looking at the graph through a small window centered at $c$. A peak inside that window can be lower than a point elsewhere on the same graph.
local.example: For $f(x)=4x^3-12x+12$ on $[-2,3]$, the graph rises and then falls at $x=-1$, giving a local maximum of $f(-1)=20$.

parts.title: What counts as nearby?
parts.definition: Choose an open interval around $c$ and restrict the comparison to domain points in that interval. At an included endpoint, compare on the side belonging to the domain.
parts.idea: At an included endpoint, the window contains graph points on only one side. Those are the points available for the local comparison.

parts.title: Classifying a critical number
parts.definition: Check whether a continuous graph rises or falls throughout each side of an interior critical number, sufficiently close to it.
parts.formula:
$\text{rises then falls}\ \Rightarrow\ \text{local maximum}$
$\text{falls then rises}\ \Rightarrow\ \text{local minimum}$
parts.idea: Trace the graph into the critical point from the left and out to the right. A reversal in direction distinguishes a peak or valley from a horizontal tangent the graph passes through.
parts.reasoning: For $p(x)=\cos x$, $p'(x)=-\sin x$ changes from positive to negative at $0$. The local maximum is $p(0)=1$.

optimization.title: Optimization
optimization.definition: The objective function is the quantity to maximize or minimize. The constraints specify which choices are allowed.
optimization.idea: Cutting larger corners gives the folding box more height but a smaller base. Both change its volume. Expressing them in terms of the same cut size lets you find where that tradeoff gives the largest box.
optimization.example: Among pairs $x,y\ge0$ with $x+y=6$, the product $xy$ has global maximum $9$ at $(3,3)$.

parts.title: Objective function and constraints
parts.definition: For the product problem, maximize the product of the two numbers subject to their given sum.
parts.idea: The given sum makes the choice of one number determine the other. Substituting the constraint turns a comparison of pairs into a problem about one variable.
parts.reasoning: With $x+y=6$ and $x,y\ge0$, $P(x)=x(6-x)$ on $[0,6]$. Compare $P(0)=P(6)=0$ with $P(3)=9$.

parts.title: Folding a box
parts.definition: Cut squares of side $x$ from the corners of a $12$-inch square. The folded box has height $x$ and square base of side $12-2x$.
parts.idea: A larger cut makes the box taller but shrinks its base. The best cut occurs where volume switches from increasing to decreasing over the allowed cuts.

figure.alt: Four corner squares of side x are marked on a 12-inch square of cardboard before it is folded.
figure.prompt: Equal squares are cut from a $12$-inch square of cardboard. Which cut produces the box of greatest volume?
figure.reasoning: For $0<x<6$, $V(x)=x(12-2x)^2$. Its derivative changes from positive to negative at $x=2$. Cutting $2$-inch squares gives an $8\times8\times2$ box with volume $128$ cubic inches.

parts.reasoning: For $0<x<6$, $V'(x)=12(x-2)(x-6)$ changes from positive to negative at $2$. The $8\times8\times2$-inch box holds $128$ cubic inches.

parts.title: Fitting a line
parts.definition: Fit $y=mx+2$ to $(0,0)$, $(1,1)$, and $(2,5)$. The slope $m$ is the choice, and the sum of squared errors $E(m)$ is the objective.
parts.idea: With the intercept fixed, only the slope can change. Completing the square shows how much extra error is incurred as the slope moves away from its best value.
parts.reasoning: $E(m)=5(m-1)^2+9$ is smallest at $m=1$. The fitted line is $y=x+2$ and the minimum sum of squared errors is $9$.

figure.alt: The three points (0,0), (1,1), and (2,5) on coordinate axes.
figure.prompt: Fit $y=mx+2$ to these three points. Which slope minimizes the sum of squared errors?
figure.reasoning: The squared errors sum to $4+(m+1)^2+(2m-3)^2=5(m-1)^2+9$. The minimum is $9$ at $m=1$.

sketch.title: Curve sketching
sketch.definition: Sketch a graph from its domain, intercepts, symmetry, asymptotes, intervals of increase and decrease, local extrema, concavity, and inflection points.
sketch.idea: A few plotted points leave many possible drawings. The asymptotes tell where the branches head, and the derivative sign graphs constrain how each branch gets there.
sketch.example: For $f(x)=\frac{x}{x+1}$, both branches increase. Only the right branch passes through the origin.

parts.title: Domain and intercepts
parts.definition: Find the domain first. Solve $f(x)=0$ within that domain for the $x$-intercepts. If $0$ is in the domain, the $y$-intercept is $(0,f(0))$.
parts.idea: Mark excluded inputs before plotting intercepts. Any point you draw has to belong to the original graph.
parts.reasoning: For $f(x)=\frac{x}{x+1}$, the domain is $\mathbb R\setminus\{-1\}$ and both axes meet the graph at $(0,0)$.

parts.title: Symmetry and periodicity
parts.definition: On a domain symmetric about $0$, an even function has $y$-axis symmetry and an odd function has origin symmetry. A period $T>0$ shifts the domain onto itself and repeats every output.
parts.idea: A reflection or a repeated piece can supply the rest of the sketch. Check the domain as well as the formula before copying a branch.
parts.reasoning: For $f(x)=\frac{2x^2}{x^2-1}$, the domain is symmetric about zero and $f(-x)=f(x)$. Reflect the sketch across the $y$-axis.

parts.title: Asymptotes
parts.definition: Check one-sided limits at breaks for vertical asymptotes. At each infinite end, look for a horizontal or slant asymptote.
parts.idea: Use one-sided limits to see what happens at a break. Then follow each branch toward infinity to see which line it approaches.
parts.reasoning: For $f(x)=\frac{x}{x+1}=1-\frac1{x+1}$, the vertical asymptote is $x=-1$ and the horizontal asymptote is $y=1$.

parts.title: Increase, decrease, and local extrema
parts.definition: Use the sign graph for $f'$ to locate intervals of increase and decrease. At an interior critical number, check whether the direction changes.
parts.idea: A break and a critical number both split the sign graph. Only an input on the graph can give a local maximum or minimum.
parts.reasoning: For $f(x)=\frac{2x^2}{x^2-1}$, split at $-1,0,1$. The excluded inputs separate branches. At $0$ the derivative changes from positive to negative, giving a local maximum of $0$.

parts.title: Concavity and inflection points
parts.definition: Use the sign graph for $f''$ to determine how each branch bends. Mark an inflection point when concavity changes at a point of continuity.
parts.idea: Use the second sign graph to bend the branches you already drew. When its sign changes, check the original curve at that input before marking a point.
parts.reasoning: For $f(x)=\frac{x}{x+1}$, the bend changes across $x=-1$. Since the curve has no point there, it has no inflection point.

parts.title: Sketch the branches
parts.definition: For $f(x)=\frac{x}{x+1}$, draw the asymptotes, plot the intercept, and trace the increasing branches.
parts.idea: The signs tell you which way each branch travels and bends. The formula tells you which side of an asymptote it occupies.

figure.alt: Two increasing branches approach the asymptotes x = −1 and y = 1, with the right branch passing through the origin.
figure.prompt: Sketch $f(x)=\frac{x}{x+1}$. Which branch approaches the horizontal asymptote from above?
figure.reasoning: Write $f(x)=1-\frac1{x+1}$. Both branches increase because $f'(x)=\frac1{(x+1)^2}>0$. The left branch lies above $y=1$. The right branch passes through $(0,0)$ and approaches $y=1$ from below.

parts.reasoning: In $f(x)=1-\frac1{x+1}$, the left branch lies above $y=1$. The right branch passes through $(0,0)$ and rises toward $y=1$ from below.

functions.title: Functions, domain, and range
functions.definition: A function assigns exactly one output to each input in its domain. Its range consists of the outputs it actually produces.
functions.idea: The formula tells you how to compute an output. The domain tells you when that computation makes sense. A tank that fills for four minutes can have a formula that still produces numbers after the water stops.

parts.title: Finding real domains
parts.definition: Find all real inputs for which the original formula is defined.
parts.idea: Check the original expression one operation at a time. In $\frac{1}{x^2-16}$, factoring the denominator reveals two excluded inputs.

parts.title: Composition of functions
parts.definition: Apply the inside function first, then apply the outside function to its output.
parts.idea: Start with $x=2$ and try the two orders from class. Add three and then square, or square and then add three. The first output becomes the next input.

parts.title: Piecewise-defined functions
parts.definition: A piecewise-defined function uses different formulas on different parts of its domain.
parts.idea: At $x=2$, look for the condition that includes equality. That single choice tells you where the filled point belongs when the two branches are drawn.

parts.title: Simplification and excluded inputs
parts.definition: Keep the original domain when canceling a common factor.
parts.idea: Use the simpler line to find the height of the missing point. Keep the exclusion from the original fraction when you draw it.

functions.example: For the tank in class, $W(t)=6+3t$ has domain $[0,4]$ minutes and range $[6,18]$ liters.

unitcircle.title: Radians and the unit circle
unitcircle.definition: An angle in standard position is measured from the positive horizontal axis. One full counterclockwise turn is $2\pi$ radians.
unitcircle.idea: Trace a point counterclockwise from $(1,0)$. Its height over one turn traces the sine graph, and its horizontal position gives the cosine at the same angle.

parts.title: Degrees and radians
parts.definition: A half-turn measures $\pi$ radians or $180^\circ$.
parts.idea: Use a half-turn as the reference. Since $\pi$ radians takes you halfway around the circle, $\pi/3$ takes you one third of that distance.

parts.title: Unit-circle coordinates
parts.definition: Cosine is the horizontal coordinate. Sine is the vertical coordinate.
parts.idea: At $3\pi/2$ the point lies directly below the origin. Read its horizontal coordinate for cosine and its vertical coordinate for sine.

parts.title: Tangent, cotangent, secant, and cosecant
parts.definition: Tangent and cotangent are ratios of sine and cosine. Secant is the reciprocal of cosine. Cosecant is the reciprocal of sine.
parts.formula:
$\tan x=\frac{\sin x}{\cos x},\quad\sec x=\frac{1}{\cos x}\quad(\cos x\ne0)$
$\cot x=\frac{\cos x}{\sin x},\quad\csc x=\frac{1}{\sin x}\quad(\sin x\ne0)$
parts.idea: At the top of the unit circle the horizontal coordinate is zero. Both $\tan x$ and $\sec x$ would divide by that coordinate, so neither is defined there.

parts.title: Amplitude and period
parts.definition: Amplitude is the distance from the midline to a peak. Period is the length of one complete cycle.
parts.idea: Sketch $\sin x$ and $3\sin x$ on the same axes. The peaks line up at the same inputs, even though one graph reaches three times as high.

infinite.title: Infinite limits and vertical asymptotes
infinite.definition: An infinite limit at $a$ means the outputs eventually exceed every positive bound, or fall below every negative bound, as $x$ approaches $a$.
infinite.idea: Near $x=-1$, a tiny denominator can make a fraction very large in magnitude. Check the sign of the whole fraction on each side to decide whether that branch rises or falls.

parts.title: Vertical asymptote
parts.definition: The line $x=a$ is a vertical asymptote if at least one one-sided limit at $a$ is infinite.
parts.idea: Trace either branch toward the suspected vertical line. In the reciprocal example, the two branches approach the same line while heading in opposite directions.

figure.alt: The two reciprocal branches approach the dashed line x = −1. One rises and the other falls.
figure.prompt: For $A(x)=\frac1{x+1}$, find the two one-sided limits at $-1$. Is there a vertical asymptote?
figure.reasoning: On the left $A(x)\to-\infty$ and on the right $A(x)\to+\infty$. The line $x=-1$ is a vertical asymptote.

parts.title: Odd and even powers
parts.definition: In $\frac{1}{(x-a)^n}$, a positive even power makes the denominator positive on both sides. A positive odd power preserves its sign.
parts.idea: Just to the left of $a$, the difference $x-a$ is negative. The exponent tells you whether that minus sign survives.

infinite.example: For $B(x)=-\frac{1}{(x+1)^2}$, both branches fall without bound at $x=-1$.

figure.alt: Both branches of negative one over the square of x plus one descend beside the vertical line x = −1.
figure.prompt: For $B(x)=-\frac{1}{(x+1)^2}$, where does each branch go as $x$ approaches $-1$?
figure.reasoning: The squared denominator approaches zero through positive values on both sides. Thus both one-sided limits are $-\infty$.

limitmethods.title: Limit strategies
limitmethods.definition: Try substitution first and check the hypotheses of the limit laws. The resulting form tells you what to try next.
limitmethods.idea: Substitution sorts the problem. A nonzero denominator gives the answer. If the denominator tends to zero, a nonzero numerator calls for a sign check on each side, while $0/0$ calls for simplification.

parts.title: Direct substitution
parts.definition: For a polynomial or rational function, substitute directly at any point in its domain.
parts.idea: Check the original denominator at the target input. When it stays nonzero, the quotient law justifies the value you get by plugging in.

parts.title: Check signs on each side
parts.definition: When the numerator tends to a nonzero number and the denominator tends to zero, check each one-sided limit.
parts.idea: Mark the sign of each factor just left and just right of the suspect input. In the class example, $x+1$ switches sign at $-1$ while the other factors keep theirs.

parts.title: Factor and cancel
parts.definition: If substitution gives $0/0$, look for a common factor. Cancel only at nearby inputs where that factor is nonzero.
parts.idea: A common factor can vanish at the target and still be nonzero at every nearby input. This lets you simplify the expression that actually determines the limit.

parts.title: Multiply by the conjugate
parts.definition: Multiply a radical difference by its conjugate to expose a factor that cancels.
parts.idea: Look for a difference of squares. Multiplying $\sqrt{x+4}-3$ by its conjugate exposes the same $x-5$ that appears in the denominator.

parts.title: Expand or remove denominators
parts.definition: For a difference quotient of form $0/0$, expand the numerator or combine its fractions.
parts.idea: In $\frac{(2+h)^2-4}{h}$ the common factor is hidden until you expand. For a difference of fractions, first give them a common denominator.

parts.title: Choosing a limit method
parts.definition: Identify the form first. Use algebra, a bound, or l’Hospital’s rule as the expression allows.
parts.idea: For $\frac{2x+\sin x}{x}$ at infinity, try dividing each numerator term by $x$. The leftover sine term is bounded, so you can decide the limit with a squeeze.

limitmethods.example: The lecture uses $f(x)=\frac{x^2-2x+1}{x^2-1}$ three times. At $2$ we plug in, at $-1$ we check signs, and at $1$ we factor and cancel.

breaks.title: Discontinuities
breaks.definition: A break occurs at $a$ when the point value is missing, the finite limit fails to exist, or the limit differs from the value.
breaks.idea: On the class graph, compare the left branch, the right branch, and the marked point at each break. Which breaks could you repair by moving just one dot?

parts.title: Removable discontinuity
parts.definition: The finite limit exists, but the value at $a$ is missing or differs from that limit.
parts.idea: The surrounding graph tells you exactly where a replacement point would go. Keep the approaching branches fixed and try filling the hole.

parts.title: Jump discontinuity
parts.definition: Both one-sided limits exist as finite numbers and give different heights.
parts.idea: Imagine moving the filled point to the other branch. The approaching heights stay separated, so changing one value cannot close the gap.

parts.title: Infinite discontinuity
parts.definition: At least one one-sided limit is $+\infty$ or $-\infty$.
parts.idea: Trace a branch toward the break. If it climbs past every height or falls below every height, there is no finite hole to fill.

breaks.example: The lecture graph has a removable discontinuity at $0$, a jump at $2$, and an infinite discontinuity at $4$.

figure.alt: At 0 there is an open circle below a filled point. At 2 the two branches approach different heights. As x approaches 4 from the left, the graph rises indefinitely.
figure.prompt: Classify the breaks at $0$, $2$, and $4$. Which one could you repair by moving a single point?
figure.reasoning: The break at $0$ is removable, the break at $2$ is a jump, and the break at $4$ is infinite. Only the hole at $0$ can be repaired by assigning its limiting height.

invtrig.title: Inverse trigonometric derivatives
invtrig.definition: On a chosen one-to-one branch, the derivative of an inverse trigonometric function is the reciprocal of the original slope at the corresponding angle, wherever that slope is nonzero.
invtrig.idea: The input is a trigonometric value and the output is an angle. Draw the angle on the chosen branch to decide which sign to use when expressing its slope in terms of the input.
invtrig.example: For $\theta=\sin^{-1}x$, the slope of the inverse is $\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}$.

parts.title: Inverse sine and inverse cosine
parts.definition: Both formulas hold for $-1<x<1$, with angles measured in radians.
parts.idea: Near $x=1$, the sine curve is almost horizontal at the angle that produces $x$. Reflecting that part of the curve explains why the inverse sine slope grows so large.
parts.aliases: arcsin arccos inverse sine inverse cosine

figure.alt: A right triangle has angle theta, opposite side x, hypotenuse 1, and adjacent side equal to the square root of one minus x squared.
figure.prompt: For $0<x<1$, let $\theta=\sin^{-1}x$. How does the triangle turn $\frac1{\cos\theta}$ into a formula in $x$?
figure.reasoning: The adjacent side gives $\cos\theta=\sqrt{1-x^2}$. Thus $\frac{d}{dx}\sin^{-1}x=\frac1{\sqrt{1-x^2}}$. The positive square root also applies on $-1<x<1$ because $\cos\theta>0$ on this branch.

parts.title: Inverse tangent and inverse cotangent
parts.definition: Both formulas hold for every real $x$. The lecture takes $\cot^{-1}x$ in $(0,\pi)$.
parts.idea: As an angle approaches $\pi/2$ from below, tangent changes very rapidly. Reversing the correspondence means that large positive inputs to inverse tangent produce smaller and smaller changes in angle.
parts.aliases: arctan arccot inverse tangent inverse cotangent

parts.title: Inverse secant and inverse cosecant
parts.definition: These derivative formulas hold for $|x|>1$ on the branches given in the lecture.
parts.idea: A value between $-1$ and $1$ cannot be the secant or cosecant of a real angle. Check the input first, then keep the absolute value when the input is negative.
parts.aliases: arcsec arccsc inverse secant inverse cosecant

tests.title: First and second derivative tests
tests.definition: Given an interior critical number $c$, determine whether $f(c)$ is a local maximum, a local minimum, or neither.
tests.idea: A critical number tells you where to look. Choose between checking how the slopes change sign and, at a horizontal tangent, checking which way the graph bends.
tests.example: For $f(x)=x\tan x$, $f'(0)=0$ and $f''(0)=2$. The second derivative test gives a local minimum at $(0,0)$.

parts.title: Fermat’s theorem
parts.definition: If $f$ has a local extremum at an interior point $c$ where it is differentiable, the tangent at $c$ is horizontal.
parts.idea: At a smooth interior peak, the nearby outputs on both sides lie below the peak. The secant slopes from the two sides can agree in the limit only at zero.

parts.title: First derivative test
parts.definition: Let $c$ be an interior critical number with $f$ continuous at $c$. Suppose $f'$ has a strict, constant sign on each side sufficiently near $c$.
parts.idea: Think of the signs as directions of travel as you move to the right. Rising into a point and falling away from it makes that point a peak.

figure.alt: A sign graph for the derivative changes from positive to negative at zero. Next to it, the parabola rises to (0,1) and then falls.
figure.prompt: Use the sign of the derivative to classify $x=0$ for $f(x)=1-x^2$.
figure.reasoning: $f'(x)=-2x$ is positive to the left of $0$ and negative to its right. The point $(0,1)$ is a local maximum.

parts.title: Second derivative test
parts.definition: Suppose $f'(c)=0$ and $f''$ is continuous on an open interval containing $c$. Its sign at $c$ gives the following conclusions.
parts.idea: At a horizontal tangent, upward bending gives a valley and downward bending gives a peak. If the second derivative vanishes there, go back to the behavior on both sides.

figure.alt: Three graphs near zero. The first passes through the origin, the second has a minimum there, and the third has a maximum.
figure.prompt: The first and second derivatives of $x^2\tan x$, $x^4$, and $-x^4$ all vanish at zero. What happens at the origin for each graph?
figure.reasoning: The second derivative test is inconclusive for all three. The first function changes sign through zero, the second has a local minimum there, and the third has a local maximum.

rationaltails.title: End behavior of rational functions
rationaltails.definition: At either infinite end, a rational function has the same limit as the quotient of its leading terms. Here $m,n$ are the degrees and $a_m,b_n$ the nonzero leading coefficients.
rationaltails.idea: Far from zero, the highest powers determine the end behavior. Reading those two terms can settle both limits before you do any polynomial division.
rationaltails.example: The leading terms of $\frac{1-x^3}{2x^3+x-1}$ give $\frac{-x^3}{2x^3}=-\frac12$. The horizontal asymptote is $y=-\frac12$.

parts.title: Compare the leading terms
parts.definition: If $m<n$ the limit is zero. If $m=n$ it is the ratio of leading coefficients. If $m>n$ the sign of the leading-term quotient determines the infinite limit at each end.
parts.idea: If a power of $x$ survives the comparison, check its sign on each end. An odd power can make one end rise while the other falls.
parts.reasoning: In the second practice problem the leading terms reduce to $-\frac{x}{2026}$. The left limit is $+\infty$ and the right limit is $-\infty$.

parts.title: Slant asymptote by division
parts.definition: When the numerator's degree is one greater than the denominator's, polynomial division gives a linear quotient. Its graph is the slant asymptote at both ends.
parts.idea: Division separates the line the graph follows from the fraction that measures its vertical difference from that line. The remainder has lower degree, so its contribution tends to zero.
parts.reasoning: Dividing $x^2$ by $x-1$ gives $x+1+\frac1{x-1}$. The slant asymptote is $y=x+1$ at both ends.

figure.alt: Polynomial long division of x squared by x minus one gives quotient x plus one and remainder one.
figure.prompt: Use polynomial division to find the slant asymptote of $g(x)=\frac{x^2}{x-1}$.
figure.reasoning: Division gives $g(x)=x+1+\frac1{x-1}$. The remainder term tends to zero at both ends, so the slant asymptote is $y=x+1$.

forms.title: Rewriting indeterminate forms
forms.definition: For an indeterminate product, difference, or power, rewrite the expression before applying l’Hospital’s rule.
forms.idea: Start by looking at the operation joining the quantities. A product can become a quotient, two fractions can share a denominator, and a logarithm can bring down a changing exponent.

parts.title: Products
parts.definition: Rewrite a product of form $0\cdot\infty$ as a quotient.
parts.idea: For $x\ln x$ near $0^+$, move $x$ downstairs as its reciprocal. Now the numerator and denominator each have a limit whose form you can check.

parts.title: Differences
parts.definition: For a difference of form $\infty-\infty$, combine fractions or multiply by a conjugate.
parts.idea: Combining the fractions in $\frac1x-\frac1{e^x-1}$ makes their cancellation visible. The two separate infinite limits cannot tell you how much is left.

parts.title: Indeterminate powers
parts.definition: For a positive base, take the logarithm of $y=f(x)^{g(x)}$ to bring down the exponent.
parts.idea: For $(1+x)^{1/x}$, taking a logarithm moves the exponent out in front. Once you know the limit of the logarithm, return to the original power by exponentiating.

forms.example: At $0^+$, $\ln\bigl((1+x)^{1/x}\bigr)=\frac{\ln(1+x)}{x}$. The logarithm tends to $1$, so the power tends to $e$.
